Practicus
ΕΥΑΓΡΙΟΥ ΜΟΝΑΧΟΥ
Ἐπειδή μοι πρώην δεδήλωκας ἀπὸ τοῦ ἁγίου ὄρους ἐν τῇ Σκίτει καθεζομένῳ,
ποθεινότατε ἀδελφὲ Ἀνατόλιε, καὶ τὸ συμβολικὸν σχῆμα τῶν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μοναχῶν
σαφηνισθῆναί σοι παρεκάλεσας· οὐ γὰρ εἰκῇ οὐδὲ παρέλκον αὐτὸ νενόμικας
τοσαύτην παραλλαγὴν ἔχον παρὰ τὰ λοιπὰ σχήματα τῶν ἀνθρώπων· φέρε, ὅσα παρὰ
τῶν ἁγίων Πατέρων περὶ τούτου μεμαθήκαμεν, ἐξαγγείλωμεν. Τὸ μὲν κουκούλλιον
σύμβολόν ἐστι τῆς χάριτος τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεοῦ σκεπαζούσης αὐτῶν τὸ
ἡγεμονικὸν καὶ περιθαλπούσης τὴν ἐν Χριστῷ νηπιότητα διὰ τοὺς ῥαπίζειν ἀεὶ καὶ
τιτρώσκειν ἐπιχειροῦντας. Ὅσοι τοίνυν ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς φέρουσι τοῦτο δυνάμει
ψάλλουσι ταῦτα· ἐὰν μὴ Κύριος οἰκοδομήσῃ οἶκον καὶ φυλάξῃ πόλιν, εἰς μάτην
ἐκοπίασεν ὁ οἰκοδομῶν καὶ ὁ φυλάσσειν πειρώμενος. Αἱ δὲ τοιαῦται φωναὶ
ταπεινοφροσύνην μὲν ἐμποιοῦσιν, ἐκριζοῦσι δὲ ὑπερηφανίαν τὸ ἀρχαῖον κακόν, τὸ
κατασεῖσαν εἰς τὴν γῆν τὸν Ἑωσφόρον τὸν πρωῒ ἀνατέλλοντα. Τὸ δὲ γεγυμνῶσθαι
τὰς χεῖρας τὸ ἀνυπόκριτον τῆς πολιτείας ἐμφαίνει· δεινὴ γὰρ ἡ κενοδοξία
συγκαλύψαι καὶ συσκιάσαι τὰς ἀρετάς, ἀεὶ δόξας τὰς παρὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων
θηρεύουσα καὶ τὴν πίστιν ἀποδιώκουσα. Πῶς γὰρ δύνασθε, φησί, πιστεῦσαι, δόξαν
παρὰ ἀλλήλων λαμβάνοντες, καὶ τὴν δόξαν τὴν παρὰ τοῦ μόνου Θεοῦ οὐ ζητοῦντες;
∆εῖ γὰρ τὸ ἀγαθὸν μὴ δι' ἕτερον ἀλλὰ δι' αὐτὸ μᾶλλον εἶναι αἱρετόν· εἰ γὰρ μὴ τοῦτο
δοθείη, φανήσεται τὸ κινοῦν ἡμᾶς πρὸς τὴν ἐργασίαν τοῦ καλοῦ πολλῷ τιμιώτερον
ὑπάρχον τοῦ γινομένου, ὅπερ τῶν ἀτοπωτάτων ἂν εἴη Θεοῦ τι κρεῖττον ἐννοεῖν τε
καὶ λέγειν. Ὁ δὲ ἀνάλαβος πάλιν ὁ σταυροειδῶς τοῖς ὤμοις αὐτῶν περιπλεκόμενος
σύμβολον τῆς εἰς Χριστόν ἐστι πίστεως ἀναλαμβανούσης τοὺς πραεῖς καὶ
περιστελλούσης ἀεὶ τὰ κωλύοντα καὶ τὴν ἐργασίαν ἀνεμπόδιστον αὐτοῖς
παρεχούσης. Ἡ δὲ ζώνη περισφίγγουσα τοὺς νεφροὺς αὐτῶν ἀπωθεῖται πᾶσαν
ἀκαθαρσίαν καὶ τοῦτο παραγγέλλει· καλὸν ἀνθρώπῳ γυναικὸς μὴ ἅπτεσθαι. Τὴν δὲ
μηλωτὴν ἔχουσιν οἱ πάντοτε τὴν νέκρωσιν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐν τῷ σώματι περιφέροντες
καὶ φιμοῦντες μὲν πάντα τὰ τοῦ σώματος ἄλογα πάθη, τὰς δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς κακίας
μετουσίᾳ τοῦ καλοῦ περικόπτοντες· καὶ πενίαν μὲν ἀγαπῶντες, πλεονεξίαν δὲ
φεύγοντες ὡς εἰδωλολατρίας μητέρα. Ἡ δὲ ῥάβδος ξύλον ζωῆς ἐστι πᾶσι τοῖς
ἀντεχομένοις αὐτῆς, καὶ τοῖς ἐπερειδομένοις ἐπ' αὐτὴν ὡς ἐπὶ Κύριον ἀσφαλής. Καὶ
τούτων μὲν σύμβολον ὡς ἐν ἐπιτομῇ τῶν πραγμάτων τὸ σχῆμα· τὰ δὲ ῥήματα ταῦτά
ἐστιν ἃ πρὸς αὐτοὺς ἀεὶ λέγουσιν οἱ Πατέρες· τὴν πίστιν, ὦ τέκνα, βεβαιοῖ ὁ φόβος ὁ
τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ τοῦτον πάλιν ἐγκράτεια, ταύτην δὲ ἀκλινῆ ποιοῦσιν ὑπομονὴ καὶ
ἐλπίς, ἀφ' ὧν τίκτεται ἀπάθεια, ἧς ἔγγονον ἡ ἀγάπη, ἀγάπη δὲ θύρα γνώσεως
φυσικῆς ἣν διαδέχεται θεολογία καὶ ἡ ἐσχάτη μακαριότης. Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ
σχήματος τοῦ ἱεροῦ καὶ τῆς διδασκαλίας τῶν γερόντων τοσαῦτα ἡμῖν ἐπὶ τοῦ
παρόντος εἰρήσθω. Περὶ δὲ τοῦ βίου τοῦ τε πρακτικοῦ καὶ τοῦ γνωστικοῦ νυνὶ
διηγούμεθα, οὐχ ὅσα ἑωράκαμεν ἢ ἠκούσαμεν, ἀλλ' ὅσα τοῦ καὶ ἄλλοις εἰπεῖν παρ'
αὐτῶν μεμαθήκαμεν, ἑκατὸν μὲν κεφαλαίοις τὰ πρακτικά, πεντήκοντα δὲ πρὸς τοῖς
ἑξακοσίοις τὰ γνωστικὰ συντετμημένως διελόντες· καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐπικρύψαντες, τὰ δὲ
συσκιάσαντες, ἵνα μὴ δῶμεν τὰ ἅγια τοῖς κυσὶ μηδὲ βάλωμεν τοὺς μαργαρίτας
ἔμπροσθεν τῶν χοίρων. Ἔσται δὲ ταῦτα ἐμφανῆ τοῖς εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ ἴχνος αὐτοῖς
ἐμβεβηκόσιν.

english: The Practicus of the monk Evagrius. You previously revealed to me, while dwelling in the Skete on the holy mountain, having desired, brother Anatolius, that the symbolic form of the monks in Egypt be made clear to you, you requested; for I have not gone over it without reason, considering it to have such a variation from the other forms of men. Come, let us declare whatever we have learned from the holy Fathers concerning this.

The hood is a symbol of the grace of our Savior God, covering their ruling faculty and sheltering the innocence in Christ against those constantly attempting to strike and lash. Therefore, those who carry this upon their head sing these things by power: 'Unless the Lord builds a house, they labor in vain who build; unless the Lord guards a city, they watch in vain who keep watch' (Ps 127:1). And such voices indeed produce humility, but they uproot pride, that ancient evil, which cast down the Morning Star rising in the morning into the earth.

And the bareness of the hands shows the sincerity of the lifestyle; for vanity is terrible, covering and overshadowing virtues, always hunting the honors from men and driving away faith. How can you, he says, believe, receiving honor from one another and not seeking the honor from the only God? For it is necessary that the good be chosen not through another but rather through itself; for if this were not given, that which moves us toward the work of the good would appear much more precious than the thing becoming, which would be among the most inexplicable things to conceive and to say of God.

And the mantle, entwined crosswise about their shoulders, is a symbol of the faith taking hold of the gentle ones, always casting aside what hinders and providing the work unhindered to them. And the belt, tightening around their loins, repels all impurity and this part...

It is announced: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. Those who always carry the death of Jesus in their body and silence all the irrational passions of the body, while cutting off the participation in the evils of the soul, possess the staff; they love poverty and flee greed as the mother of idolatry. The staff is the wood of life to all who hold fast to it, and to those who lean upon it as if upon a secure Lord. The shape of these things is a symbol as a summary of the realities; these words are what the Fathers always say to them: the fear of God makes faith firm, and again self-control makes this firm, and patience and hope make it unshakeable, from which apathy is born, of which love is the offspring, and love is the door to natural knowledge which theology receives and the ultimate blessedness.

Let enough be said to us regarding the form of the holy and the teaching of the elders in the present matter. But concerning the life of both the practical and the contemplative, we now discourse, not as much as we have seen or heard, but as much as we have learned to say to others from them, passing through the practicals abbreviated in one hundred chapters and the contemplatives in fifty toward the six hundred; having highlighted some and shadowed others, so that we might not give holy things to dogs nor cast our pearls before swine (Matt 7:6). These things will be manifest to those who have stepped into the same track.

σφοδρότερος τοῖς ἐγκρατευομένοις ἐφίσταται, ἵν' ὡς μηδὲν ἀνύοντες παύσωνται·

ἐν τῇ λύπῃ βαπτίζουσιν ὡς οὐχ ὑπαρχόντων τῶν προτέρων πραγμάτων οὐδὲ
δυναμένων λοιπὸν διὰ τὸν παρόντα βίον ὑπάρξαι· καὶ ἡ ταλαίπωρος ψυχή, ὅσον
διεχύθη ἐπὶ τοῖς προτέροις λογισμοῖς, τοσοῦτον ἐπὶ τοῖς δευτέροις συνεστάλη
ταπεινωθεῖσα.

english: One struggles to encounter [them]. Indeed, desire for every pleasure begins with desire, but sensation gives birth to desire, for sensation is without part and free from passion. For the recluses, the demons fight naked, but for those working out virtue in communities or companionships, they arm the less attentive of the brothers; and the second war is much more dull than the first, because it is not possible to find on the earth men more bitter than demons or all of them constantly receiving their malice.

Concerning the eight logismoi: Eight are all the most general logismoi in which every logismos is contained. First is that of gluttony, and after it that of fornication; third is that of avarice; fourth is that of sorrow; fifth is that of anger; sixth is that of acedia; seventh is that of vainglory; eighth is that of pride. Whether to disturb all these in the soul or not to disturb them is not up to us; but to delay them or not to delay them, or to move passions or not to move them, is up to us.

The logismos of gluttony subjects the monk of asceticism to a rapid fall: stomach and liver and spleen and fluids being disordered, and a long disease, and scarcity of the necessary things, and the helplessness of physicians. And it often brings to mind for him certain brothers having fallen into these passions. And there is a time when even comparing those who have suffered them discourages those exercising self-control, and causes them to recount their own misfortunes, and how from asceticism such people have become.

The demon of fornication compels bodies to desire diversely; and he stands against those exercising self-control more fiercely, so that they might cease without any relief; and he bends the thoughts down, defiling the soul concerning those, making her say certain words and again hear, as if she had seen once and the matter were present. Avarice subjects long old age and weakness of hands toward work, and famines and diseases occurring together, and the bitterness of poverty, and how it is painful to receive from others.

Regarding things related to need. 10 Sorrow sometimes happens by deprivation of desires, and sometimes it follows anger. By deprivation of desires it happens thus: certain thoughts, having gone before, lead the soul into the memory of house and parents and former lifestyle. And when, not having resisted it but following it, they saw it being poured out in pleasures according to the intellect, then taking it in sorrow, they baptize it as if the former things did not exist and were not able to exist anymore through the present life; and the wretched soul, as much as it was poured out upon the former thoughts, so much it was contracted, having been humbled, upon the second ones.

11 Anger is a sharper passion; for it is called a heat and a movement of the spirit against the one who has done wrong or is thought to have done wrong; which all day long indeed makes the soul savage, but especially in the prayers snatches away the mind, reflecting the face of the one who has been grieved. And it, while lingering and changing into wrath, provides disturbances by night, exhaustion of the body and paleness, and attacks of wild beasts' venomous strikes. These four things, happening after the wrath, anyone would find accompanied by more thoughts.

12 The demon of acedia, who is also called the noonday demon, is the heaviest of all demons; and he stands over the monk around the fourth hour, and circles his soul until the eighth hour. And first he makes seeing the sun difficult or motionless, showing the day as fifty hours. Then he is compelled to constantly look toward the doors and to leap out of the cell, staring at the sun how much of the ninth hour has remained, and looking here and there lest any of the brothers be near. english: Desiring to encounter bodies, which one must not obey, but rather do the opposite.

Do not give yourself to the thought of anger, fighting the one who is saddened by thought; nor again imagine more pleasure for the thought of fornication; for the one watches over the soul, while the other calls the soul toward the burning of passion; both make your mind dirty. And imagining idols even at the time of prayer and not offering a pure prayer to God, you immediately fall to the demon of acedia, who most especially falls into such states and tears the soul like a prey like a dog.

The nature of anger is to fight with demons and to struggle for some pleasure. Therefore, the angels, presenting to us spiritual pleasure and blessedness from this, urge us to turn our mind toward the demons; but they again, drawing us toward worldly desires, force the mind to fight against humans by nature, so that the mind, being darkened and falling away from knowledge, becomes a traitor to the virtues.
Take care of yourself lest you provoke any of the brothers to flee, and you may not drive away the demon of sorrow in your life, which becomes a stumbling block to you always at the time of prayer.
Gracious gifts extinguish grudges; and let Jacob persuade Esau, having come with gifts after four hundred, going out to meet him. But we, being poor, let us satisfy the need at the table.

When we fall to the demon of acedia, who divides the soul in such a way with tears, let us make the one part entreating and the other part being entreated, promising good hopes to ourselves and looking to the holy David: 'Why are you so sorrowful, my soul, and why are you disquieting me? Hope in God, for I shall still praise Him; the salvation of my face and my God.'
It is not necessary during the time of trials to leave the cell, feigning reasonable excuses, but to remain within.

To stand firm, to endure, and to receive all things that come bravely, but to exclude entirely the demon of acedia, which being the heaviest above all, most rigorously works upon the soul. For fleeing such struggles and surrounding the mind clumsily teaches one to be cowardly and a deserter.

And our holy and most practical teacher said: Thus the monk must always prepare himself as if he were to die tomorrow, and again to use the body as if he were to live in it for many years. For the former, he says, cuts off the thoughts of acedia and prepares the monk more urgently; the latter preserves the body and always maintains its temperance equally.

It is difficult to escape the thought of vainglory; for what you do toward its destruction, this becomes for you a beginning of another vainglory. And not against every thought of ours do the demons oppose, but also some of these evils occur according to which we are accustomed.

I recognized the demon of vainglory to be pursued by almost all among the demons, and shamelessly standing over the falls of those pursuing virtue, making manifest to the monk a greatness of virtues. He who has grasped knowledge and reaps the pleasure from it will no longer be persuaded by the demon of vainglory, even when bringing to him all the pleasures of the world; for what could he promise greater than spiritual contemplation? Insofar as we are without knowledge, we eagerly work out the practical life, showing our purpose to God that we do all things for the sake of His knowledge.

Remember your former life and the ancient failings, and how being moved by passion, you passed over to the Christ-like apathy, and how again you came out of the world which has much and much a times humbled you. And consider this for me too: who is the one guarding you in the desert, and who is the one driving away the demons, gnashing their teeth against you? For such thoughts indeed produce humility, but they do not admit the demon of pride.

For those in the world, the demons struggle more through external things, but for the monks, more so through thoughts; for through external things they are lacking because of the desert. english: Through dreams we come to know things. And we say that apatheia is a health for the soul, and knowledge is its nourishment, which alone is accustomed to join us to the holy powers, if indeed the union with the incorporeal things is destined to come from a similar disposition.

There are two peaceful states of the soul: one is produced from the natural seeds, the other is acquired from the withdrawal of the demons. To the former, humility with compunction follows, and a tear and an infinite longing toward the Divine, and an immeasurable zeal for the work; to the latter, vainglory with pride, drawing the monk down through the destruction of the other demons. Therefore, he who keeps the boundaries of the former state will more keenly recognize the attacks of the demons.

The demon of vainglory opposes the demon of fornication, and for a soul that is not able to withstand them both at once, one is promised honor while the other brings dishonor. Whichever of these, having approached, presses you, you have perhaps formed the thoughts of the opposing demon within yourself; even if you are able to expel the proverbial 'leek from the soil,' know that you are near the boundaries of apatheia; for your mind is strong enough to annihilate the thoughts of demons with human thoughts. But to repel the thought of vainglory through humility, or the thought of fornication through sobriety, would be the deepest evidence of apatheia. And try to do this against all the adversaries through various demons; for you will also know more clearly which passion you have overcome. Furthermore, ask from God whatever power is needed to defend against the enemies in the second way.

As much as the soul advances, so much greater adversaries it receives; for I am not persuaded that the same demons always remain with it; and this is known most by those who impose themselves more keenly upon the temptations, and see the apatheia approaching them being snatched away by those who have received it. Perfect apatheia in the soul approaches through the victory over all the adversaries in the practical struggle against the demons; but imperfect apatheia is called that which is toward the power of the total overcoming of the former demon.

Even if the mind were to depart on that beautiful journey, and become among the incorporeal ones in the land, it would not succeed without correcting its inner things; for the disturbance of the inner things tends to turn it back toward those from which it had departed.
Both virtues and vices work the mind blind: the former so that it may not see vices; the latter so that it may not see virtues again.
Regarding the signs of apatheia: When the mind begins to perform the prayers without distraction, then a war is established regarding the thymic part of the soul, both at night and with the day.
A sign of apatheia is when the mind, having begun to see the inner light, remains quiet and smooth in observing things, even toward the phantasms of sleep.
The mind is strengthened when it imagines nothing of this world except during the time of prayer.

Having achieved practical [living] with God and having approached the knowledge, the mind is seized by knowledge as a lever, separating it from the sensible things, grasping a little or even not at all of the rational part of the soul.
A soul has apatheia, not one that does not suffer regarding things, but one that remains undisturbed even regarding their memories.

Great indeed is to pray without distraction, but greater is to also sing without distraction.

He who has established the virtues within himself, and having been fully strengthened by these, no longer remembers law or commandments or punishment, but says and does whatever the best state dictates.

english: To acquire wisdom without war is impossible, and one cannot win the war without prudence; for this prudence is believed to stand against the passion of the demons, forcing the powers of the soul to act according to nature and making the way of wisdom easy. 74 A temptation is merely a thought ascending through the passive part of the soul and darkening the mind. 75 Sin is merely the assent of the thought toward a forbidden pleasure. 76 Angels rejoice when evil is diminished, but demons when virtue is; for the former are servants of mercy and love, while the latter are obedient to anger and hatred; and the former, approaching us through spiritual contemplation, fill us, while the latter, approaching, cast shameful fantasies into the soul. 77 Virtues do not stop the impulses of the demons, but they preserve us innocent. 78 Practical method is a spiritual method that cleanses the passive part of the soul. 79 The working of the commandments is not sufficient to perfectly heal the powers of the soul, unless the mind also receives contemplations suitable to them. 80 It is not possible for us to resist all the thoughts cast at us by angels, but it is possible to overthrow all the thoughts from demons; for a peaceful state follows the former thoughts, but a disturbed one follows the latter. 81 Love is the offspring of apatheia; and apatheia is the flower of practice; and practice is established by the keeping of the commandments; and the guardian of these is the fear of God, which is the offspring of right faith; and faith is a ready good, which is in its nature to exist even in those who do not yet believe in God. 82 Just as the soul acting through the body is affected by weak members, so the mind, acting, recognizes its own proper energy and its own powers, and discovers through that which obstructs it its own therapeutic commandment. 83 The mind, fighting the passionate war, will not perceive the reasons of the war; for it is like one fighting in the night; but having acquired apatheia, it will easily recognize the methods of the enemies. 84 The end of practice is love; the end of knowledge is theology; the beginnings of both are faith and natural contemplation; and as many as

On the one hand, demons touch the passive part of the soul, and these are said to oppose practice; but those who wander again in the rational part are named enemies of all truth and contrary to contemplation. The bodies of those being purified do not join with those who are purified; but the virtues both purify the soul and remain with the purified.

By nature, the rational soul acts when its desiring part yields to virtue, its spirited part struggles on its behalf, and its rational part applies itself to the contemplation of realities. He who progresses in practice diminishes the passions, while he in contemplation diminishes ignorance; for of the passions there shall one day be a total destruction, but of ignorance, some say there is an end, while others say there is none.

Virtues and vices become creative through their use beyond mere utility; the use of these for other ends belongs to prudence. Since the rational soul is threefold according to our wise teacher, when virtue arises in the rational part, it is called prudence, understanding, and wisdom; when in the desiring part, temperance, love, and self-control; and when in the spirited part, courage and endurance; but in the whole soul, justice. And the work of prudence is to strategize against the opposing powers, to defend the virtues, to array oneself against the vices, and to manage the intermediate things according to the seasons; of understanding, to harmoniously manage all things contributing to us toward the goal; of wisdom, to contemplate the reasons of bodily and incorporeal things; of temperance, the work is to look apathetically at the things that move irrational imaginations within us; of love, to make oneself such an image of God in every respect that it is almost the prototype, even if demons attempt to defile them; of self-control, to abstain from all pleasure of the throat with joy; of endurance and courage, to not fear enemies and to bravely withstand the terrible; of justice, to produce a certain concord and harmony of the parts of the soul.
Seeds produce drops of moisture, but virtues produce knowledge; and just as tears follow the seeds, so joy follows the drops.

Death of the father was announced to one of the monks; but to the one who announced it, he says, stop blaspheming; for my father is immortal.
One of the brothers desired that one of the elders, having passed by the house, would command the mother and sisters to eat him; but he, with a woman, said, you shall not eat.

One of the brothers had only the gospel, and having sold this, he gave it for food to those who were hungry, declaring a word worthy of remembrance: for I, he says, have sold the very word that says to me: sell your possessions and give to the poor (Luke 12:33).

english: On one hand, it is not possible to love brothers equally, but it is possible to encounter them apathetically while being prone to grudges and free from hatred. One must love priests along with the Lord, those cleansing us through the holy mysteries and praying for us; and one must honor our elders as if they were angels, for they are the ones anointing us for the struggles and healing the wounds of wild beasts.

But now, let these things be said to you regarding practice, most desiring brother Anatolius, as many things as we have found by conversing while the grace of the Holy Spirit is occasionally falling upon the vine as we scatter the seed. And if the sun shall strike us steadily and the grape becomes experienced, then we shall also drink its wine which gladdens the heart of man (Ps 104:15), through the prayers and intercessions of the righteous Gregory who planted me and of the now-holy Fathers who water me, and by the power of Christ Jesus our Lord who grows me, to whom be glory and dominion for the ages of ages (Rev 1:6).
